Period schedule:

Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Hidden Digits: Place Value in Decimals

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 12.2 p.69

time_bands.activity: Students write the number 27.53 in expanded form, naming tens, units, tenths, and hundredths aloud. The class compares readings to confirm the place-value structure that extends the Indian number system beyond the ones place.

Working in pairs, students convert spice-mass fractions — 50 g, 100 g, 25 g, 250 g expressed as fractions of a kilogram — into decimals by writing equivalent fractions with denominators 10, 100, and 1000. They note how many decimal places each denominator produces.

Students explore the divide-by-power-of-ten pattern: starting from 123 ÷ 10, 24 ÷ 100, 12 ÷ 1000, and 12345 ÷ 1000, they write each result, count the zeroes in the divisor, count the places the point moves left, and record the pattern in a table.

Class discusses the generalised rule — place the decimal point at the end, move left by as many places as there are zeroes — and checks whether inserting leading zeroes is sometimes needed, using 24 ÷ 100 = 0.24 as the test case.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the number of zeroes in the divisor with the position of the decimal point rather than the direction of movement; watch for answers like 24 ÷ 100 = 2.4 instead of 0.24. The spice-mass fractions and the divide-by-power-of-ten pattern are designed to surface the same rule from two directions, strengthening the connection between fraction equivalence and decimal notation. Example 1, section 12.2 p.69 is a natural bridge to the next section if students finish early.
materials: Blank charts or squared paper for place-value tables

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 12.2 p.73–74
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete a table multiplying 5.7, 23.02, 0.92, 0.306, and 24.67 by 10, 100, and 1000.

time_bands.activity: Students play the Jonali-and-Pallabi fraction–decimal game in pairs: one student writes a fraction with denominator 10, 100, or 1000 on a slip of paper; the other converts it to a decimal and reads it aloud naming every place-value position. Roles switch after each round.

The class works through the spice context in reverse — given a decimal such as 0.025 kg, students write the fraction form, identify the denominator, and state which metric prefix it corresponds to. Several pairs share answers and reconcile differences.

Figure it Out Q10, section 12.2 p.73–74 ("Complete a table multiplying 5.7, 23.02, 0.92, 0.306, and 24.67 by 10, 100, and 1000.") is used as a structured drill: students fill the table and then write the general rule in their own words.

Quick whole-class check: teacher reads out five decimal–fraction pairs and students hold up slips labelled T (terminating, finite decimal) or F (fraction form only), justifying their choice by naming the denominator's prime factors.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the decimal place-value structure and the power-of-ten rule, this unit applies them in a game context that keeps conversion active rather than passive. Watch for students who multiply instead of moving the point when scaling by 10 — they may not yet see the shortcut as the same operation. Figure it Out Q10, section 12.2 p.73–74 doubles as a preview of the decimal-multiplication digit-count rule students will derive in the next section.
materials: Blank paper slips for the game
T/F cards or folded paper labels

periods.activity_title: From Fractions to Products: Building the Multiplication Rule

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 12.2 p.69
Example 2, section 12.2 p.69
textbook_items_in_class.description: A car travels 12.5 km per litre; distance on 7.5 litres = 12.5 × 7.5 = (125×75)/(10×10) = 9375/100 = 93.75 km.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 3, section 12.2 p.70
textbook_items_in_class.description: Ajay walks 827 m (0.827 km) each way to school, twice a day, 6 days a week: 0.827 × 2 = 1.654 km/day, and 1.654 × 6 = 9.924 km/week.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 4, section 12.2 p.70
textbook_items_in_class.description: Area of a rectangle with sides 5.7 cm and 13.3 cm = 5.7 × 13.3 = (57×133)/100 = 7581/100 = 75.81 sq cm.

time_bands.activity: Example 1, section 12.2 p.69 ("Arshad buys 5 pens at ₹9.5 each....") is worked through with the class: students convert 9.5 to a fraction, multiply, and re-read the answer as a decimal. The connection between the fraction denominator and the number of decimal places in the product is noted on the board.

Students work Example 2, section 12.2 p.69 ("A car travels 12.5 km per litre; distance on 7.5 litres....") and Example 3, section 12.2 p.70 ("Ajay walks 827 m (0.827 km) each way to school....") in pairs, writing both factors as fractions, multiplying, and recording in a three-column table: decimal places in first factor | decimal places in second factor | decimal places in product.

Example 4, section 12.2 p.70 ("Area of a rectangle with sides 5.7 cm and 13.3 cm....") is added to the table. Students scan all four rows and articulate the pattern — the product's decimal places equal the sum of the factors' decimal places — in their own words.
Students write and read out the general rule, then verify it instantly on 5.7 × 13.3 by computing 57 × 133 = 7581 and placing the point two places in from the right to get 75.81.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error here is counting the decimal places in the product by position from the left rather than from the right; watch for 75.81 written as 7.581. Working through Examples 1–4 as a table-building exercise keeps the induction visible: students derive the rule from their own accumulated evidence rather than memorising it. Example 5, section 12.2 p.72 is a concise self-study consolidation for students who want to verify the rule on a fresh pair of decimals.
materials: Squared paper or ruled notebooks for the table

periods.activity_title: Greater or Smaller? Reasoning About Decimal Products

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 12.2 p.73
Figure it Out Q9, section 12.2 p.73
textbook_items_in_class.description: Without multiplying, decide which products are less than 1: (a) 7 × 0.6; (b) 0.7 × 0.6; (c) 0.7 × 6; (d) 0.07 × 0.06.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.2 p.73
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the products in tenths, hundredths, etc.: (a) 6 × 4 tenths; (b) 7 × 0.3; (c) 9 × 5 hundredths.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 12.2 p.73

time_bands.activity: The class revisits the three situations — both factors greater than 1, both between 0 and 1, and one of each — through a quick conjecture round: students predict whether each product in Figure it Out Q9, section 12.2 p.73 ("Without multiplying, decide which products are less than 1....") is less than 1 or not, and write a one-sentence reason before computing.

Figure it Out Q8, section 12.2 p.73 ("Given 18 × 12 = 216, find (a) 18 × 1.2; (b) 18 × 0.12; (c) 1.8 × 1.2; (d) 0.18 × 0.12; (e) 0.018 × 0.012; (f) 1.8 × 12, and state which products are less than 1.") is worked individually. Students then tabulate each sub-part against the three situations and check whether their earlier conjecture held.

Figure it Out Q1, section 12.2 p.73 ("Find the products in tenths, hundredths, etc.: (a) 6 × 4 tenths; (b) 7 × 0.3; (c) 9 × 5 hundredths.") is tackled, with students naming the unit (tenths, hundredths) and connecting it to the fraction-form multiplication already established.

Pairs share their reasoning on which products are less than 1 and why, articulating the generalisation: a product is less than 1 when both factors lie strictly between 0 and 1. The teacher invites counter-examples to test the boundary cases.

periods.teacher_notes: Having derived the digit-count rule for decimal multiplication, students now reason about the size of the result, mirroring fraction-multiplication behaviour. A common error is assuming that multiplication always makes things larger; the discussion of both-factors-between-0-and-1 is the key corrective. Figure it Out Q2, section 12.2 p.73 is set as homework to consolidate the placement rule on fresh three-digit decimals.
materials: Blackboard for tabulating the three situations

periods.activity_title: Sharing Ribbons and Regrouping: Division with Decimals

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 6, section 12.3 p.74
textbook_items_in_class.description: Anuja cuts a 3.9 m ribbon into 10 equal pieces: 3.9 ÷ 10 = (39/10) × (1/10) = 39/100 = 0.39 m each (and into 100 pieces gives 0.039 m).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 7, section 12.3 p.75–76
Example 8, section 12.3 p.77
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 1324 ÷ 4 by division using place value (long division), regrouping thousands into hundreds, etc.: 1324 ÷ 4 = 331.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 9, section 12.3 p.81
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 237 ÷ 8 by long division with a decimal quotient, regrouping ones into tenths, tenths into hundredths, hundredths into thousandths: 237 ÷ 8 = 29.625.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.3 p.83
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the quotient by converting the denominator into 1, 10, 100, or 1000 and verify by long division: (a) 18/5; (b) 415/4; (c) 1217/2; (d) 4827/8.

time_bands.activity: Example 6, section 12.3 p.74 ("Anuja cuts a 3.9 m ribbon into 10 equal pieces....") is posed as a problem students solve before the solution is revealed. The move-the-point-left shortcut is connected to the power-of-ten division rule from section 12.1.

Example 7, section 12.3 p.75–76 ("29 m of ribbon shared by 2....") and Example 8, section 12.3 p.77 ("Find 1324 ÷ 4 by division using place value....") are worked in sequence, with students tracking when they regroup ones into tenths and where the decimal point appears in the quotient.

Example 9, section 12.3 p.81 ("Find 237 ÷ 8 by long division with a decimal quotient....") extends the procedure to a case where regrouping continues into hundredths and thousandths. Students work through the algorithm step by step and confirm the answer is 29.625.

Figure it Out Q1, section 12.3 p.83 ("Find the quotient by converting the denominator into 1, 10, 100, or 1000 and verify by long division: (a) 18/5; (b) 415/4; (c) 1217/2; (d) 4827/8.") is begun individually; at least parts (a) and (b) are completed in class with both the equivalent-fraction method and the long-division check.

periods.teacher_notes: The critical step students miss is placing the decimal point in the quotient at the moment they first regroup ones into tenths — watch for quotients that are whole numbers when a decimal answer is expected. Moving from equivalent-fraction division (Example 7) to place-value long division (Examples 8 and 9) builds the bridge so neither technique feels arbitrary. Example 10, section 12.3 p.82 is a good self-study item for students who want to practise the algorithm on a decimal dividend.
materials: Squared paper for place-value long-division layout

periods.activity_title: Decimal Divisors and the Art of Making Them Whole

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 10, section 12.3 p.82
textbook_items_in_class.description: A shopkeeper packs 9.5 kg of sugar equally into 4 bags: 9.5 ÷ 4 = 2.375 kg per bag, placing the decimal point before dividing the tenths.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 11, section 12.3 p.83
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 0.06 ÷ 5 by place value: 0 ones, 0 tenths, 6 hundredths give 1 hundredth with remainder regrouped into thousandths, so 0.06 ÷ 5 = 0.012.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 12, section 12.3 p.84
textbook_items_in_class.description: Ravi covers 126 km in 2.5 hours; average speed = 126 ÷ 2.5. Converting the divisor: 126 × (10/25) = 1260/25 = 50.4 km/h.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 13, section 12.3 p.84
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 4.68 ÷ 1.3 and 4.68 ÷ 0.13 by making the divisor a whole number: multiply dividend and divisor by the same power of ten, so 4.68 ÷ 0.13 = 468 ÷ 13.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 12.3 p.83
Figure it Out Q2, section 12.3 p.86
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the quotients (a) 24.86 ÷ 1.2; (b) 5.728 ÷ 1.52.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 12.3 p.83

time_bands.activity: Example 10, section 12.3 p.82 ("A shopkeeper packs 9.5 kg of sugar equally into 4 bags....") and Example 11, section 12.3 p.83 ("Find 0.06 ÷ 5 by place value....") are worked, with particular attention to where the decimal point is placed in the quotient when the dividend itself is a decimal.

Figure it Out Q3, section 12.3 p.83 ("Find the quotient (a) 132 ÷ 4; (b) 13.2 ÷ 4; (c) 1.32 ÷ 4; (d) 0.132 ÷ 4.") is worked as a structured set, students observing how the quotient's decimal point shifts as the dividend's point shifts, connecting to the scalar relationship.

Example 12, section 12.3 p.84 ("Ravi covers 126 km in 2.5 hours....") and Example 13, section 12.3 p.84 ("Find 4.68 ÷ 1.3 and 4.68 ÷ 0.13 by making the divisor a whole number....") introduce the decimal-divisor strategy: multiplying both dividend and divisor by the same power of ten. Students articulate why the quotient is unchanged.

Figure it Out Q2, section 12.3 p.86 ("Find the quotients (a) 24.86 ÷ 1.2; (b) 5.728 ÷ 1.52.") is attempted, applying the decimal-divisor strategy and performing the resulting whole-number long division.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who multiply only the dividend — not both dividend and divisor — by the power of ten when clearing a decimal divisor, which changes the quotient. The scalar relationship established in Examples 12–13 (dividing by 0.13 is the same as dividing by 13 then multiplying by 100) mirrors the fraction operation already known, so linking explicitly to that knowledge reduces errors. Figure it Out Q4, section 12.3 p.83 is set as homework to reinforce the pattern of shifting the decimal point in the dividend.

periods.activity_title: When Does Division Ever End? Exploring Repeating Decimals

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.3 p.86
textbook_items_in_class.description: Express in decimal form: (a) 2/5; (b) 13/4; (c) 4/50; (d) 5/8.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 12.3 p.86–87
Figure it Out Q4, section 12.3 p.87

time_bands.activity: Students divide 10 by 3 using long division, recording each remainder. After five steps they observe that the remainder is always 1 and the digit 3 repeats without end. The class discusses: why does this happen, and what does it mean for the decimal expansion?

Students divide 1 by 7 step by step, recording the sequence of remainders: 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1, … They notice the cycle of length 6, read off the repeating block 142857, and multiply 142857 by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 to discover the cyclic-permutation pattern — the 'magic number'.

Figure it Out Q1, section 12.3 p.86 ("Express in decimal form: (a) 2/5; (b) 13/4; (c) 4/50; (d) 5/8.") is worked, and students classify each result as terminating or non-terminating, then state the denominators in terms of their prime factors (2s and 5s only → terminating).

Figure it Out Q4, section 12.3 p.87 ("Evaluate (a) 25 ÷ __ = 0.025; (b) 25 ÷ __ = 250; (c) 25 ÷ __ = 2.5; (d) 25 ÷ 10 = 25 × __; (e) 25 ÷ 0.10 = 25 × __; (f) 25 ÷ 0.01 = 25 × __.") is used to articulate the dividend–divisor–quotient relationship, including expressing division by a decimal as multiplication by its reciprocal.

periods.teacher_notes: The discovery that 1 ÷ 7 produces a cyclic remainder sequence is the conceptual high point of the division section; students who merely memorise 0.142857 miss the reasoning about why the cycle exists and why it has length 6. Emil Artin's 1927 conjecture — that infinitely many primes generate such full-length cycles — can be mentioned as an open problem to pique curiosity without requiring proof. Watch for students who assume any repeated digit signals a mistake in their long division rather than a property of the fraction.
materials: Optional: calculators for cycle verification only

periods.activity_title: Word Problems and Unit Conversions: Decimal Division in Action

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 12.3 p.87
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the quotient (a) 2.46 ÷ 1.5; (b) 2.46 ÷ 0.15; (c) 2.46 ÷ 0.015, and decide whether 24.6 ÷ 1.5 equals 2.46 ÷ 0.15.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 12.3 p.87
textbook_items_in_class.description: 3 litres of watermelon juice is shared equally among 8 friends; find each share in millilitres.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 12.4 p.94
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the blanks using the given conversions: 5.5 km = __ m; 35 cm = __ m; 14.5 cm = __ mm; 68 g = __ kg; 9.02 m = __ mm; 125.5 ml = __ l.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: A 210 g packet of peanut chikki costs ₹70.5 and a 110 g packet of potato chips costs ₹33.25; decide which is cheaper (per gram).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 12.3 p.87
homework.description: A car covers 234.45 km using 12.6 litres of petrol; find the distance travelled per litre.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q5, section 12.3 p.87 ("Find the quotient (a) 2.46 ÷ 1.5; (b) 2.46 ÷ 0.15; (c) 2.46 ÷ 0.015, and decide whether 24.6 ÷ 1.5 equals 2.46 ÷ 0.15.") is worked in pairs, with students explaining in writing why scaling both parts by the same factor preserves the quotient.

Figure it Out Q8, section 12.3 p.87 ("3 litres of watermelon juice is shared equally among 8 friends; find each share in millilitres.") requires a unit conversion (litres to millilitres) before dividing; students identify and carry out the conversion as a separate step.

Figure it Out Q5, section 12.4 p.94 ("Fill the blanks using the given conversions: 5.5 km = __ m; 35 cm = __ m; 14.5 cm = __ mm; 68 g = __ kg; 9.02 m = __ mm; 125.5 ml = __ l.") is worked, with students deciding for each blank whether to multiply or divide by a power of ten and stating the conversion factor.

Figure it Out Q1, section 12.4 p.93 ("A 210 g packet of peanut chikki costs ₹70.5 and a 110 g packet of potato chips costs ₹33.25; decide which is cheaper per gram.") introduces unit-price comparison: students compute cost-per-gram for each packet and justify their choice.

periods.teacher_notes: The transition from section 12.3's word problems to section 12.4's applied contexts is seamless here — both demand choosing the correct decimal operation and identifying the right unit before computing. Watch for students who compare total prices rather than unit prices in the chikki-vs-chips question; the error reveals a conceptual gap about what 'cheaper' means in a per-unit sense. Figure it Out Q9, section 12.3 p.87 (the car-petrol problem) is set as homework since it parallels the unit-price reasoning in class.

periods.activity_title: Leap Years, Shelves, and Profit: Decimal Arithmetic in Context

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 12.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shyamala buys 3 kg of bananas at ₹30/kg, counts 35 bananas, and sells each at ₹5; find her profit on selling all.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 12.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Textbooks 2.5 cm thick are placed on a 160 cm shelf; find how many of 80 books fit and whether any space is left.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 12.4 p.94
textbook_items_in_class.description: Sridharacharya's Patiganita problem: 6¼ divided by 2½ and 60¼ divided by 3½; solve by converting the fractions into decimals.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 12.4 p.94
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the boxes in at least 2 different ways: (a) __ × __ = 2.4; (b) __ × __ = 14.5.

time_bands.activity: The Earth's year of 365.2422 days is used to motivate decimal multiplication: students compute 0.2422 × 100 to find how many extra days accumulate over a century, then reason why adding a leap day every four years over-corrects. The divisibility-decision chart (divisible by 4? by 100? by 400?) is built on the board.

Figure it Out Q3, section 12.4 p.93 ("Shyamala buys 3 kg of bananas at ₹30/kg, counts 35 bananas, and sells each at ₹5; find her profit on selling all.") and Figure it Out Q4, section 12.4 p.93 ("Textbooks 2.5 cm thick are placed on a 160 cm shelf; find how many of 80 books fit and whether any space is left.") are worked in pairs — both require identifying whether to multiply or divide before computing.

Figure it Out Q6, section 12.4 p.94 ("Sridharacharya's Patiganita problem: 6¼ divided by 2½ and 60¼ divided by 3½; solve by converting the fractions into decimals.") is worked, first converting each mixed number to a decimal and then dividing using the decimal-divisor strategy.

Figure it Out Q7, section 12.4 p.94 ("Fill the boxes in at least 2 different ways: (a) __ × __ = 2.4; (b) __ × __ = 14.5.") is explored as an open-ended investigation: students find multiple factor pairs, including pairs where one factor is a decimal less than 1, and share the most surprising solution.

periods.teacher_notes: The leap-year calculation shows decimal multiplication as a tool for correcting a cumulative error — a powerful context for why precision matters in arithmetic. Watch for students who round 365.2422 to 365.25 before computing; the approximation is acceptable only if students can articulate what precision they are sacrificing. Sridharacharya's Patiganita problem offers a historical cross-curricular moment worth a brief mention of the 9th-century text.

periods.activity_title: Patterns, Quotients, and Termination: Reasoning Through Decimal Structure

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 12.4 p.94
Figure it Out Q9, section 12.4 p.94
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill in the missing cells of a table where each cell represents a ÷ b, given values 1517, 151.7, 15.17, 1.517, 15170 and divisors 37, 3.7, 0.37.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 12.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write the decimal number at each arrow mark on the given number lines (between 3.1 and 3.2, and between 2.15 and 2.17).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 12.4 p.94
homework.description: Fill in the missing cells of a table where each cell represents a ÷ b, given values 1517, 151.7, 15.17, 1.517, 15170 and divisors 37, 3.7, 0.37.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q8, section 12.4 p.94 ("Given 756 ÷ 36 = 21, find (a) 75.6 ÷ 3.6; (b) 7.56 ÷ 0.36; (c) 756 ÷ 0.36; (d) 75.6 ÷ 360; (e) 7560 ÷ 3.6; (f) 7.56 ÷ 0.36.") is worked, students writing a one-sentence justification for each sub-part explaining how the decimal shifts in dividend and divisor interact.

Figure it Out Q2, section 12.4 p.93 ("Write the decimal number at each arrow mark on the given number lines between 3.1 and 3.2, and between 2.15 and 2.17.") is worked, requiring students to reason about the scale of each sub-interval and place decimals precisely, connecting division of the interval to the decimal structure.

The table of 1/2, 1/(2×2), … and 1/5, 1/(5×5), … is revisited: students fill entries, state whether each terminates, and construct the general claim — a fraction terminates as a decimal if and only if its denominator (in lowest terms) has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. They test the claim on 2/5, 13/4, and 1/6.

Figure it Out Q9, section 12.4 p.94 ("Fill in the missing cells of a table where each cell represents a ÷ b, given values 1517, 151.7, 15.17, 1.517, 15170 and divisors 37, 3.7, 0.37.") is introduced and partially begun; students identify the scalar relationships before completing the table as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The termination claim about denominators built from 2s and 5s is the chapter's deepest piece of reasoning; students should be asked to explain why 1/6 does not terminate (the denominator 6 = 2 × 3 contains a 3) rather than only verifying by long division. Watch for students who think any decimal that goes on 'many places' is non-terminating — they may need to compute 1/8 = 0.125 as a counterexample to that intuition. Figure it Out Q9, section 12.4 p.94 is set as homework since the table's scalar pattern rewards unhurried exploration.
materials: Number-line diagrams (drawn on board or squared paper)

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly shows how the decimal 0.045 is read using place-value names?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 hundredths and 5 thousandths (option B). The digit 4 sits in the hundredths place and the digit 5 sits in the thousandths place, giving 4/100 + 5/1000 = 0.040 + 0.005 = 0.045.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify each digit's position in the decimal place-value table: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student shifted the decimal one place too far left, reading the tenths and hundredths positions instead of the hundredths and thousandths.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student collapsed both digits into a single tenths unit, treating 0.045 as if it were 4.5 tenths — a place-value confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student misread the ones column as an active digit place, confusing the leading zero with a value-bearing digit.

inclusivity.support: Let the student write 0.045 in a place-value table with columns labelled ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths and read off each column.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write two more decimals that have a zero in the tenths place and name all non-zero place values in each.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 12.2 p.73–74
exercise.description: Complete a table multiplying 5.7, 23.02, 0.92, 0.306, and 24.67 by 10, 100, and 1000.

items.prompt: Priya says that the product of 0.4 and 0.3 must be greater than both 0.4 and 0.3 because multiplication makes numbers bigger. Is Priya correct? Explain your reasoning using what you know about multiplying fractions or decimals between 0 and 1.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya is incorrect. When both factors lie strictly between 0 and 1, the product is smaller than either factor. Here, 0.4 × 0.3 = (4/10) × (3/10) = 12/100 = 0.12, which is less than both 0.4 and 0.3. Multiplying by a number less than 1 scales the other factor down, not up.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert each decimal to a fraction over a power of ten, multiply numerators and denominators, and compare the product with each original factor.

inclusivity.support: Invite the student to think aloud with a partner: 'What is half of 0.4?' to build the intuition that a fraction of a decimal is smaller.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if one factor is between 0 and 1 and the other is greater than 1, is the product always between the two factors? Explore with an example and explain.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 12.2 p.73

items.prompt: When Divya divides 1 by 3 using long division, she notices that the remainder after every step is always 1. She wonders whether the decimal will ever end. Explain why the decimal expansion of 1 ÷ 3 never terminates, using what you know about remainders in long division and about which fractions give terminating decimals.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The decimal 1 ÷ 3 never terminates because the remainder after dividing is always 1 — each new step just brings down a zero and divides 10 by 3 again, giving quotient digit 3 and remainder 1 forever. A decimal terminates only when the remainder eventually becomes 0. Since 3 is not a factor of any power of 10, no stage of the division produces remainder 0; equivalently, the denominator 3 contains the prime factor 3 (neither 2 nor 5), so no equivalent fraction with a denominator that is a power of 10 can be formed.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Track the remainder at each stage of long division and connect non-zero repeating remainders to the prime factors of the denominator.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to write out the first four steps of dividing 1 by 3 and circle each remainder — the pattern becomes visible quickly.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: does 1 ÷ 7 also never terminate? What is the length of its repeating cycle, and why is the cycle length at most 6?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.3 p.86

items.prompt: Rohit is told that 840 ÷ 42 = 20. He then tries to find 8.40 ÷ 0.42 without computing from scratch. Explain how he can use the given fact to find the answer, and justify why his method gives the correct quotient.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 8.40 ÷ 0.42 = (8.40 × 100) ÷ (0.42 × 100) = 840 ÷ 42 = 20. Multiplying both dividend and divisor by the same number (here 100) does not change the quotient, because division measures how many times one quantity fits into another, and scaling both by the same factor leaves that ratio unchanged. So the answer is 20.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply dividend and divisor by the same power of ten to convert to a whole-number division whose result is already known.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to think of a simpler analogy: if 10 ÷ 5 = 2, does 100 ÷ 50 also equal 2? Why?
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what is 84.0 ÷ 0.042? Does multiplying both parts by 1000 still use the given fact, and what adjustment if any is needed?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 12.4 p.94

items.prompt: A shopkeeper has a 1 kg bag of cardamom. A customer buys 250 g. Write 250 g as a fraction of 1 kg, then convert that fraction to a decimal by writing an equivalent fraction whose denominator is a power of 10. What decimal does 250 g represent in kilograms?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write the mass as a fraction over 1000, simplify, then read off the decimal by matching the denominator to a power of ten.

inclusivity.support: Provide a place-value table with columns labelled ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths and ask the student to place the digits of 250/1000.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to express 175 g and 375 g in kilograms as decimals, and to spot a pattern in the answers.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 12.2 p.73–74
exercise.description: Complete a table multiplying 5.7, 23.02, 0.92, 0.306, and 24.67 by 10, 100, and 1000.

items.prompt: A rectangular garden has a length of 8.4 m and a width of 3.5 m. Find its area in square metres by converting each measurement to a fraction over a power of ten, multiplying, and placing the decimal point using the digit-count rule.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 8.4 = 84/10 and 3.5 = 35/10. Product = (84 × 35)/(10 × 10) = 2940/100 = 29.40 = 29.4 sq m. Verification by digit-count rule: 8.4 has 1 decimal place, 3.5 has 1 decimal place; total = 2 places; 84 × 35 = 2940, placing point 2 from the right gives 29.40 = 29.4. Both methods agree.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert decimals to fractions over powers of ten, multiply numerators, sum decimal places for point placement.

inclusivity.support: Let the student first draw and label the rectangle, then remind them that area = length × width before setting up the multiplication.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the length is scaled to 8.40 m (adding a trailing zero), does the product change? Why or why not, and what does this reveal about trailing zeros in decimals?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.2 p.73
exercise.description: Find the products in tenths, hundredths, etc.: (a) 6 × 4 tenths; (b) 7 × 0.3; (c) 9 × 5 hundredths.

items.prompt: A 29 m length of rope is to be cut into 4 equal pieces. Using an equivalent fraction whose denominator is 100, find the length of each piece as a decimal. Then verify your answer using long division.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 29 ÷ 4 = 29/4. To make the denominator 100: 29/4 = (29 × 25)/(4 × 25) = 725/100 = 7.25 m. Verification by long division: 4 goes into 29 seven times (28), remainder 1; regroup 1 one as 10 tenths, 4 goes into 10 twice (8), remainder 2; regroup 2 tenths as 20 hundredths, 4 goes into 20 five times exactly. Quotient = 7.25. Both methods agree.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Form an equivalent fraction with denominator 100 by multiplying numerator and denominator by 25, then read the decimal; verify with place-value long division.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to first check: does 4 divide evenly into 100? If yes, what must the multiplier be?
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: can you find the length using denominator 1000 instead of 100? Do you get the same decimal, and what does that tell you about equivalent fractions?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.3 p.83
exercise.description: Find the quotient by converting the denominator into 1, 10, 100, or 1000 and verify by long division: (a) 18/5; (b) 415/4; (c) 1217/2; (d) 4827/8.

items.prompt: Find the value of 16.8 ÷ 4 using place-value long division. Show clearly where you place the decimal point in the quotient and what happens when you regroup ones into tenths.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 16.8 ÷ 4: 4 goes into 16 four times (16), remainder 0. Place decimal point. Bring down the 8 tenths; 4 goes into 8 twice. Quotient = 4.2. Verification: 4.2 × 4 = 16.8. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the whole-number part first; when you bring down the tenths digit, place the decimal point in the quotient and continue dividing.

inclusivity.support: Provide a blank long-division frame with the decimal point position marked, so the student sees where to insert it before they begin.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what if the dividend were 16.80 (written with a trailing zero)? Does the quotient change? Use this to discuss why trailing zeros after the last non-zero digit do not affect value.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 12.3 p.83

items.prompt: Find 3.75 ÷ 0.25. Show how you convert the divisor into a whole number and then carry out the division.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply dividend and divisor by the same power of ten to make the divisor a whole number, then divide normally.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to first decide: how many decimal places does 0.25 have? What power of ten must you multiply by to clear those places?
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what is 3.75 ÷ 0.025? Without recomputing from scratch, can you use the result of 3.75 ÷ 0.25 to find it quickly?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 12.3 p.87
exercise.description: Find the quotient (a) 2.46 ÷ 1.5; (b) 2.46 ÷ 0.15; (c) 2.46 ÷ 0.015, and decide whether 24.6 ÷ 1.5 equals 2.46 ÷ 0.15.

items.prompt: A 500 g packet of mixed nuts costs ₹187.50 and a 350 g packet of the same nuts costs ₹130.55. Find the cost per gram for each packet (to the nearest hundredth of a rupee) and state which is the better buy.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide total price by mass in grams for each packet and compare the unit prices.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student first convert each price to paise (multiply by 100) and each mass to grams — working in whole numbers — before dividing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: by how many paise per gram is one packet cheaper? If you bought 1 kg of nuts, how much would you save by choosing the cheaper packet?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.4 p.93
exercise.description: A 210 g packet of peanut chikki costs ₹70.5 and a 110 g packet of potato chips costs ₹33.25; decide which is cheaper (per gram).

items.prompt: A vegetable seller buys 5 kg of tomatoes at ₹18.50 per kg. She sorts them and discards 0.5 kg as damaged. She sells the remaining tomatoes at ₹25 per kg. Find her total cost, total revenue, and profit or loss.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute total cost using decimal multiplication, subtract discarded mass to find quantity sold, multiply by selling price, then find profit as revenue minus cost.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to write out three separate steps — cost, quantity sold, revenue — before attempting to find profit, so the structure is clear.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what selling price per kilogram would she need to set to make a profit of exactly ₹30, given the same cost and the same quantity discarded?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 12.4 p.93
exercise.description: Shyamala buys 3 kg of bananas at ₹30/kg, counts 35 bananas, and sells each at ₹5; find her profit on selling all.
